This formulation allows the model to handle variable-length inputs and outputs without requiring a pre-specified alignment. The use of LSTM is motivated by its ability to learn long-range temporal dependencies, which are necessary because of the time lag between input and corresponding output tokens. The model estimates the conditional probability of the output sequence given the input sequence by factorizing it into per-token probabilities, each conditioned on the fixed vector and previously generated tokens. This representation is a key antecedent to later attention-based models, which address its limitations for long sequences.
limits: The fixed-length vector may be a bottleneck for very long sentences.
The model cannot handle out-of-vocabulary words.
relevant_contributions.problem: Standard DNNs require fixed-dimensional inputs and outputs, but many tasks like translation involve sequences of unknown length with complex, non-monotonic relationships.

relevant_contributions.explanation: The paper introduces layer normalization as a transposition of batch normalization: instead of normalizing each neuron's summed input using mean and variance estimated over a mini-batch of training cases, it computes these statistics over all hidden units in a layer for each individual training case. This removes the dependency on mini-batch size, allowing pure online learning with batch size 1, and avoids the need for separate statistics per time step in recurrent networks. The method also provides invariance to re-scaling of individual training cases and to re-scaling and re-centering of the entire weight matrix, as shown in the invariance analysis. Empirically, layer normalization speeds up training and improves generalization in RNNs, particularly for long sequences and small mini-batches, and is robust to batch-size variations in feed-forward networks.
limits: Layer normalization is not invariant to individual weight vector scaling, unlike batch normalization.
In convolutional networks, layer normalization underperforms batch normalization because hidden units near image boundaries have different statistics.
The paper does not provide a formal proof of convergence benefits; relies on empirical evidence.
relevant_contributions.problem: Batch normalization depends on mini-batch size and is hard to apply to recurrent neural networks, where statistics vary across time steps and test sequences may be longer than training ones.

relevant_contributions.explanation: The paper proposes that instead of encoding the entire source sentence into a single fixed-length vector, the decoder should compute a distinct context vector for each target word. This context vector is a weighted sum of encoder annotations, where weights are computed by an alignment model that scores the relevance of each source position to the current target word. The alignment model is a feedforward neural network trained jointly with the rest of the system. This soft attention mechanism allows gradients to flow through the alignment computation, enabling end-to-end training. It also provides a way to visualize alignments, which are shown to be linguistically plausible, including non-monotonic alignments for reordering.

relevant_contributions.explanation: The paper proposes multi-head attention, where instead of a single attention function, the queries, keys, and values are linearly projected h times with different learned projections to lower dimensions. Attention is then performed in parallel on each projected version, and the outputs are concatenated and projected again. This allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, counteracting the averaging effect of single-head attention. The total computational cost is similar to single-head attention with full dimensionality due to reduced dimensions per head.

reviews.rationale: The supplementary equations apply layer normalization to LSTM gates/cell states and GRU components, preserving the base method as the recurrent special case.
The paper describes using a gated hidden unit with update and reset gates, attributed to Cho et al. (2014a), and notes it is similar to LSTM. This is in Appendix A.1.1.
The analysis shows self-attention has O(1) path length, which motivates the architecture's ability to learn long-range dependencies. The passage supports this.

The paper reports constituency parsing results with 91.3 F1 on WSJ only and 92.7 F1 semi-supervised, outperforming many previous models and the BerkeleyParser in the small-data regime. The passages support the claim.

The paper reports the ensemble of 5 deep LSTMs achieving 34.81 BLEU versus 33.30 for the SMT baseline, and states this is the first time a pure neural system outperforms a phrase-based SMT baseline on a large-scale task.
p17 states each encoder layer has a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network as its second sub-layer, so the feed-forward network is a genuine component of the Transformer layer.
The paper describes masking in decoder self-attention to prevent attending to future positions, ensuring the auto-regressive property. The passages support the claim.
The paper presents examples of attention heads exhibiting interpretable behavior, supporting the claim that self-attention can yield more interpretable models. The passage supports this.

The supplementary material provides specific equations for applying layer normalization to LSTM and GRU, extending the basic method to recurrent gating structures. The cited passages contain these formulations, so the generalized_by edge is warranted.
The paper describes sharing the weight matrix between embedding layers and the pre-softmax transformation as part of the model. The passage supports this.
The gated hidden unit is used in the RNNs of the attention-based model, as described in Appendix A.1.1.

p6 abstract states the Transformer 'generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data'; p104 frames parsing as a generalization test; p96/p101 give 91.3 WSJ-only and 92.7 semi-supervised; p108 says it outperforms BerkeleyParser with only WSJ 40K sentences. The premise (parsing success) bears on the conclusion (versatility/generalization).
The Transformer architecture is built on multi-head self-attention layers, as described in the paper. The passage supports this.
The ablation study in row (E) shows nearly identical results for sinusoidal and learned positional embeddings. The passage supports this.
The paper introduces sinusoidal positional encodings, explains their purpose, and attributes the parameter-free position representation to Noam Shazeer. The passages support the claim.
The paper provides a comparative analysis of self-attention, recurrent, and convolutional layers in terms of complexity, sequential operations, and path length. The passages support the claim.
Since the Transformer has no recurrence or convolution, positional encodings are added to inject order information. The passage supports this.
The paper describes position-wise feed-forward networks with two linear transformations and ReLU, equivalent to kernel-size-1 convolutions. The passages support the claim.
Multi-head attention is defined as parallel applications of the attention function, which is scaled dot-product attention. The passage supports this premise.

The paper explicitly introduces layer normalization as computing mean and variance over all hidden units in a layer for a single training case, contrasting with batch normalization's mini-batch statistics. It states that layer normalization imposes no constraint on mini-batch size and can be used with batch size 1, and that it is straightforward to apply to RNNs without per-time-step statistics. The invariance properties and empirical benefits are also described in the cited passages.

The paper presents examples of attention heads exhibiting interpretable behavior related to syntax and semantics, such as long-distance dependencies and anaphora resolution. The passages support the claim.
The path-length analysis (O(1) max path length for self-attention) is an argument bearing on the conclusion that the architecture can learn long-range dependencies, matching the stated warrant.
The state-of-the-art BLEU scores on translation tasks validate the architecture's design. The passage supports this.
The decoder self-attention is masked to prevent attending to future positions, as described in the architecture. The passage supports this.

The paper provides algebraic derivations and a table summarizing invariance properties: layer normalization is invariant to re-scaling of individual training cases and to re-scaling and re-centering of the entire weight matrix, while batch normalization is invariant to weight vector re-scaling and dataset re-centering. These claims are directly supported by the text.
The paper reports BLEU scores of 28.4 on En-De and 41.8 on En-Fr, outperforming previous models including ensembles, with lower training cost. The passages support the claim.

The paper defines scaled dot-product attention with the formula softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V and explains the scaling rationale to avoid small gradients for large d_k. Attribution to Noam Shazeer is explicitly stated.
The paper describes multi-head attention with parallel projections, concatenation, and final projection, and attributes the proposal to Noam Shazeer. The passages provide full support.

The supplementary material provides explicit equations for layer-normalized LSTM and GRU, applying LN to gate pre-activations and cell states with separate gain and bias parameters. The text describes the formulations and initialization choices, directly supporting the claim.

The passage defines multi-head attention as performing the attention function in parallel on projected queries/keys/values, and Figure 2 labels that function as scaled dot-product attention, so scaled dot-product attention is the core premise/component of multi-head attention.

The paper reports ablation results showing single-head attention is worse, reducing key size hurts quality, bigger models are better, dropout helps, and positional encoding type has negligible impact. The passages support the claim.

p58 states 'self-attention could yield more interpretable models' and that attention heads 'learn to perform different tasks' related to syntactic/semantic structure, directly supporting the interpretability claim.
The paper describes sharing the weight matrix between embedding layers and the pre-softmax transformation, and multiplying embedding weights by sqrt(d_model). The passage supports the claim.
The Transformer uses scaled dot-product attention in its multi-head attention layers, as described in the architecture. The passage supports this.
p6 Table 2 shows rescoring the baseline 1000-best with an ensemble of 5 reversed LSTMs gives 36.5 versus baseline 33.30, matching the claim that the LSTM rescoring improves BLEU.

The paper explicitly claims the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention, without recurrence or convolution, and reports superior translation quality with greater parallelizability and less training time. The passages directly support these claims.

The paper's invariance analysis frames the subsequent Riemannian metric study, connecting normalization to implicit learning rate reduction. The cited passages show that the geometric analysis builds on the normalization framework, so the premise_for edge is justified.

p3 states 'we used two different LSTMs: one for the input sequence and another for the output sequence' within the fixed-vector scheme, directly grounding the premise that separate encoder/decoder LSTMs are part of the model.
Row (E) ablation replaces sinusoidal positional encoding with learned positional embeddings and observes 'nearly identical results to the base model,' directly supporting the claim.
p18 says the decoder self-attention is masked 'to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions,' ensuring predictions depend only on earlier known outputs.

The paper uses the Fisher information matrix and Riemannian metric to analyze normalized GLMs, showing that normalization scalars implicitly reduce learning rate as weight norms grow and that learning gain parameters in normalized models depends only on prediction error magnitude, making them more robust to input scaling. The cited passages contain these derivations and conclusions.
Each encoder and decoder layer includes a position-wise feed-forward network in addition to attention. The passage supports this.
The paper contrasts its attention mechanism with Graves' handwriting alignment, noting that Graves' is monotonic and insufficient for translation reordering. This is in Section 6.1.

The paper defines layer normalization and then derives its invariance properties from that definition, providing theoretical grounding. The passages cited contain both the definition and the invariance analysis, so the support edge is warranted.

The paper explicitly proposes a differentiable attention mechanism that computes a weighted sum of encoder annotations for each target word, with an alignment model trained jointly. This is directly described in Section 3 and the abstract.

The paper explicitly describes using one LSTM to read the input sequence into a fixed-dimensional vector and another LSTM to decode the target sequence, with the conditional probability factorization. This is the core method presented.
The paper shows that the same LSTM can be used to rescore SMT n-best lists, improving BLEU further, indicating the model's utility beyond direct translation.
p12 states 'For the activation function f of an RNN, we use the gated hidden unit recently proposed by Cho et al. (2014a),' documenting use of the gated unit in the attention model's RNN.
The paper uses two separate LSTMs for encoding and decoding, which is a design choice within the fixed-vector approach.
p78 reports the big Transformer outperforming prior models including ensembles by >2.0 BLEU, a new state of the art of 28.4, and lower training cost, directly supporting the empirical finding.
The paper reports that rescoring the 1000-best lists with the LSTM improves BLEU to 36.5, using an even average of scores.
p16 states the Transformer uses stacked self-attention layers, making multi-head attention a component premise of the architecture.
The paper states that two different LSTMs are used for input and output sequences, increasing parameters at negligible cost and facilitating multi-language training.
The paper compares its attention to Graves' alignment, noting the difference in monotonicity.

p3 states layer normalization 'make[s] it invariant to re-scaling all of the summed inputs to a layer,' and p2/p3 define the method and its normalization scalars, grounding the invariance claim in the definition.
p8 explicitly compares to Graves (2013) and states 'The main difference from our approach is that... the modes... only move in one direction,' a concrete limited correspondence.

p42 states the model has no recurrence/convolution, so to use sequence order 'we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position'; this is the stated premise for needing positional encodings.

p4 presents the invariance results (Table 1) and then states 'In this section, we analyze learning behavior through the geometry and the manifold of the parameter space,' framing the Riemannian metric analysis as following from the invariance investigation; p5 develops the Riemannian metric and implicit learning-rate reduction.
p21 describes scaled dot-product attention as the attention used in the architecture; the Transformer's multi-head attention is built from it, so it is a component premise.
p41 states the same weight matrix is shared between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation, with embedding weights multiplied by sqrt(d_model).
